parts.why: Three matches per card, no capitals in the rows, matches spread across positions; keys right.

The direction says 'Draw a line from each capital letter to its small letter', but each card is a capital, an arrow and a row of three small letters, and the key RINGS the answer. A line from Z across u and a to z cannot be scored cleanly. Change the direction to 'Circle the small letter that matches the capital letter.' Balance: B uses look-alike distractors (Q among q g o; A among y a e) while A's Z among u a z has none; give A one look-alike too (e.g. Z among s z x, L among i l t).

Direction only: 'try one on your own on the empty line' — there is no empty line; each card is one line with a model, three dashed letters and blank space at its right end (where the key writes E/P/I/H). Say 'at the end of the line'. Letters and stroke dots are right; A (E, P) and B (I, H) are of similar difficulty.
Keys c d / h i and e h / q s are right and unique; same kind in both forms.

Check B: the 'peach' picture (enlarged) is a red, round fruit with a long stem and a leaf; a US kindergartner calls it an apple. Swap in a clear peach (fuzzy, orange-pink, with the crease) or pick another 5-letter picture word that cannot be misnamed. Check A moose is clear.
dog/jam/hen/cap each match one picture; distractors (eye, can, fan, bed, jar, ear, ham, leg) start with other letters; pictures read as named.

Each box holds ONE word, so the child copies it onto the line without reading anything (A: are, we; B: for, the). It does not check sight-word reading. Put both of the form's words in each box (A: 'are  we'; B: 'for  the'); then only one fits each sentence (The kids are at school / Today we read a book; I made a hat for my doll / I can see the moon).

The 'many' side has only the dashed word 'whales' (B: 'lemons') to trace, so 'One or many? Trace the word that names more than one' offers no choice and tests nothing about adding -s. Print two words under the group (whale / whales; lemon / lemons) and have the child circle the one that names them, or print dashed 'whale' with an empty box for the -s.

The answer depends on the word the child says. Check B 'avocado' (enlarged: a halved avocado with its pit) is often unknown to US kindergartners or called a pear ('a pear' would be marked wrong); B is also harder than A (elephant, cat). Replace avocado with an an-word every K child names (egg, apple, owl), and have the teacher name each picture (direction below). Raspberry ('a berry') is safe.

Not a sort: in every card the picture is an exact copy of one bin's label picture (A: wolf → wolf/donkey, horse → reindeer/horse; B: plum → plum/apricot, kiwi → pomegranate/kiwi), so it is identical-picture matching. Also the B 'plum' reads as a red apple and the 'apricot' as an orange. Label the two bins with categories (e.g. 'animals' with a cow icon, 'fruit' with a banana icon) and give each card an item NOT shown on a bin (wolf → animals; kiwi → fruit), mixing which bin is right.

Check B: the 'big' dog and the 'small' dog are the same puppy drawing at almost the same size, and the right answer is the only option showing the same object, so a child matches dog to dog without knowing the opposite. Use two different objects with a clear size contrast (big elephant → small mouse) or another pair whose answer picture differs from the prompt (hot sun → cold snowflake, with 'cold' then removed from the distractors). Check A (heavy elephant → light feather) is right.
Snowman (1 4 2 3) and cake (2 4 3 1) orders are right and unique; only the direction's 'each story' should be singular (see instruction).
cat/hat/bat and lock/pan/fan are right, one fit each; pictures (padlock, frying pan, electric fan, the animal bat) read as named; positions vary.

Forms differ: A (fish, duck) needs the digraphs sh and ck in one box; B (dog, pig) is plain CVC with one letter per sound, so B is easier. Give each form one digraph word and one plain word (A: fish, pig; B: ship or shell, dog), or two of each kind. Also the B 'dog' is a cartoon puppy; a child who says 'puppy' fills four boxes and is marked wrong — have the teacher name each picture (direction below).

horse (or + silent e), zebra (final schwa), lemon (schwa o) and apple (pp + -le) are not Grade 1 spelling patterns, and the key note asks for the correct spelling after the unit, so most first graders lose both points for 'hors', 'zebru', 'lemin', 'apul' — which L.1.2.e says they should write. Use Grade 1 spellable words of equal length in both forms (A: frog, nest; B: crab, drum — or plant, skunk), or score every form by sounds in order.

Answer tell: all four words have two syllables (rab-bit, dol-phin, rac-coon, pan-da), so a child who draws two scoops every time scores full marks. Mix the counts in each form, e.g. A: rabbit (2) and elephant (3) or cat (1); B: panda (2) and butterfly / kangaroo (3) or dog (1).

The picture beside each sentence IS the answer (meerkat, helicopter, motorcycle, bicycle), so the child matches picture to bank word without reading the sentence. Show a small picture for every bank word instead (cat, meerkat, seal...), not one beside the sentence. Then also replace A box 1, which needs knowledge of meerkats rather than reading ('The ___ stands up tall to look out for danger'), with a sentence a first grader can solve from the words, e.g. 'The ___ swims and claps its flippers.' (seal).

Check A: the sentence is 'I can see two ducks.' but the picture shows ONE duckling. Show two ducks (or change the sentence to 'I can see a duck.' with the words reshuffled). B 'Where is the pear?' and its picture are right; both have one order only.

Keys right (Where/Who; Where/What), but every small picture works against the sentence (enlarged): a chef at a stove for 'Leo is at the pool', an adult florist for 'Emma plays in the tent', a barber for 'Eli plays in the cabin'. The same finding was made in the last review. Remove the pictures or use a plain child figure in the named place.
Apple core (A) and finished paper chain (B) are the only fits; the direction's 'each story's' should be singular (see instruction).
horse leopard orangutan swan = 4 2 3 1 and clementine mango pineapple watermelon = 2 4 1 3 are right; distinct first letters in both forms.

One word per form and both are nouns (turtle, cherry): a 50/50 guess, and verbs are never tested. Give each form four words, two nouns and two verbs (A: turtle, jump, cherry, sing; B: frog, run, apple, swim), with different words in A and B.
they/she and they/he are right; pictures fit the names.

Check B: both words take 'a' (lime, pineapple), so no 'an' word is tested and writing everything under 'a' scores full marks; A has one of each (elephant/an, dog/a). Make B one of each, e.g. lime (a) and orange (an).
quiet, found, bad, healthy are the only opposites; the synonym traps (noisy, missing, great, ill) work.

Check B box 2 pairs surprised with 'astonished', a Grade 3+ word; A's pairs are cheerful/happy and small/little. Replace 'astonished' with 'amazed' so both forms are at Grade 1 level. Other pairs are right and single.
big < huge < gigantic and tap < knock < bang are right; the direction's 'each row' should be 'the row' (see instruction).
starry (star) and fishy (fish) are the only words built from the picture word; stack/stair and fist/first are good look-alikes.

Check B: 'mia glued the persimmon on the paper' is an odd sentence (gluing a fruit to paper) with an unfamiliar word, and the persimmon picture reads as a tomato. Use a common thing, e.g. 'mia glued the leaf on the paper'. Check A is fine (US speakers would more often say 'learn about dolphins').

One word per form (A: red, B: eat): a 1-in-3 guess, nouns are never tested, and A and B test different word classes. Give each form three to six words with at least one noun, one verb and one adjective (A: kite, jump, red; B: lamp, eat, soft).

All four plurals are regular -s (ducks, balls, horses, lions) — a Grade 1 skill. The Grade 2 lesson (L.2.1.b) is irregular plurals plus -es. Keep one regular word and add one irregular or -es word per form, e.g. A: ducks + mice (three mice); B: horses + feet / boxes, with matching pictures and counts.

Check A box 1 'Lily ___ in the garden today. (run)': 'ran' is equally right ('today' can be earlier today) and 'is running' is more natural. Also A tests only present -s (runs, wanders) and B only past (shouted, sang), so the forms differ and A never checks the Grade 2 irregular past. Give each form one present and one irregular past: A 'Every day Lily ___ in the yard. (run)' runs + 'Yesterday Mia ___ to the park. (go)' went; B 'Every day Tom ___ at the zoo. (shout)' shouts + 'Last night Mia ___ for an hour. (sing)' sang. ('yard' is the US word where a child runs.)
He→Oliver, She→Naomi; He→Elijah, She→Sofia; the numbered key marks show it.

Keys and the note accepting 'What time...?' are right, but the small pictures contradict the sentences: a police officer for Leo, a janitor for Eli, a guitar player for 'Tom reads at the playground', a waitress for 'Lily plays'. Remove them or use plain child figures. Optional: 'Eli sleeps at six o'clock' reads oddly; 'Eli goes to bed at eight o'clock' is more natural.

Check A's answer (face → a_e) is the same pattern as the worked example printed in the rule box (cake), so the child can copy it; B's answer (flute → u_e) is not shown. Use an o_e word in A (bone, rose), or drop the worked examples from both. The flute picture (enlarged) reads as a flute; fl_t_ makes it clear.
pain and rest are the only shared roots; 'empty stone' should be 'empty box' (see instruction).

Keys right and single, but A is harder than B (amazed → astonished, weep → cry vs powerful → strong, big → large), and B reuses A's words as distractors (amazed, tasty, peaceful). Replace A box 1 with a pair at B's level (e.g. shout → yell) and use fresh distractors in B.

Check A: '"Oh please, just five more minutes in the pool," Lily ___.' — the key wants 'asked', but 'complained' is just as defensible (a child whining for more time), and the line is not a question. Use 'begged' as the answer with distractors that cannot fit (warned, yawned, laughed), or make the line a question ('"Can we stay five more minutes?" Lily ___.' → asked, with warned / yawned / promised). Check B (yawned) is right and single.

A and B use the SAME story ('The Garden') with one question each, so a retake on B is a re-read of a known text, and B (a morning/evening trap) is harder than A (a rabbit, stated once). Give B its own story of the same length, and ask two questions per form (one who/what, one when/why). Also US English: 'her little green can' reads as a food can — write 'watering can'.
elephant/giraffe/monkey and dolphin/seagull/sailboat are unique; picture order does not follow sentence order.

Only one row, 'Legs', and the penguin picture shows its two legs, so the answer is read off the picture (A) with no reading. Use rows that need the fact sheet or knowledge (body covering: feathers / fur / scales; eats: fish / grass / seeds) and two or three rows per form.
US spelling: the direction says 'grey letters'; it must be 'gray'. Content fine (w in A is a slightly harder join than u in B, acceptable).

Check B box 1 'like': 'unlike' is a real word a third grader can defend as the opposite (like/unlike), besides the key's 'dislike'. Replace 'like' with a word that takes only one prefix (honest → dishonest, obey → disobey). Also in- is never the answer in either form; make one item per form an in- word (correct → incorrect, complete → incomplete) and tell the child to choose the prefix (direction below).
One word per form (hop → go; spy → look): a 50/50 guess. Give each form four words, two per field (A: hop, stroll, peek, stare; B: dash, wander, spy, glance).
photographer/dancer and baker/runner are right; same spelling load (add -er, drop e, double n). 'empty brick' should be 'empty box' (see instruction).

The direction ('Write the four words above each stone into the sentences below it, one word in each gap') does not fit the card: one sentence, one gap, four choices, and the root sits in a banner, not a stone. Change the direction (below). Keys playfulness / helpfulness are the only good fits.

checks.why: A fair check of five of the seven lessons; fix the apple-looking peach and the two directions that describe marks and lines the cards do not have.
Word-to-picture matching is good, but the sight-word part is copying and the one-and-many part is tracing, so two of four lessons are not really checked until the cards offer a choice.
Story order is good; the sorting part is identical-picture matching and B's opposite is dog-to-dog, so two of three parts must change before the check measures the unit.
Word families are fine; sound boxes are unequal across forms, the spelling words are not Grade 1 patterns, and every syllable answer is 2.
All keys are right, but the pictures give away part 1 and contradict parts 2 and 3; with those pictures fixed it is a fair check of four of five lessons.
All eight lessons are now checked and most parts are right; the noun/verb part is a one-word coin toss and B's a/an part has no 'an' word.

Pronouns and capitals are fine; the word-class part is one word, the plurals and verb forms miss the Grade 2 irregular forms (and A's verb has two right answers), and the question-part pictures mislead.
Root words are fine; the 'said' item in A has two defensible answers, the synonym forms are unequal, and A's spelling answer is shown as the worked example.
Both forms read the same story with one question, and the fact sheet is answerable from the picture; fix those and 'grey'.
Person words and root-word forms are right; the go/look part is a one-word coin toss, B's 'like' has two answers, and part 4's direction describes a different card.

instruction.K-222: Circle the small letter that matches the capital letter.
instruction.K-238: Trace each letter. Then write one on your own at the end of the line. Start at the orange dot and follow the arrows.
instruction.K-389: Read the sentence. Write the word from the box that fits on the line.
instruction.K-302: Look at the picture with more than one. Circle the word that names them.
instruction.K-288: I will say the name of each picture. Circle a or an to go in front of it.
instruction.K-379: Look at what changes in the story. Write 1, 2, 3 and 4 in the boxes to put the pictures in order.
instruction.G1-312: I will say the name of each picture. Say the word slowly. Write the letter or letters for each sound in its own box. Start at the left. Leave the boxes you do not need empty.
instruction.G1-305: I will say the name of each picture. Clap its parts. Draw one scoop under every syllable you hear.
instruction.G1-350: Read the sentence. Find the word in the word bank that fits and write it in the box.
instruction.G1-400: Look at the three pictures in the story, then circle the picture below that belongs in the ? frame.
instruction.G1-293: Read each word. Is it a noun or a verb? Write it in the right bin.
instruction.G1-396: Read the three words in the row. Write 1, 2 and 3 in the boxes, from the weakest word to the strongest.
instruction.G2-317: Read each sentence and the verb in parentheses. Write the right form of the verb in the box.
instruction.G2-254: Read the story carefully. Then circle the best answer to each question.
instruction.G2-375: Circle the part the three words share and write that root word in the empty box.
instruction.G2-377: Trace the gray letters, then keep writing the letter joined on your own to the end of the line and on the empty line below.
instruction.G2-320: Choose un-, dis- or in- for each word. Write the new word that means the opposite on the line.
instruction.G3-398: Look at each person, read the word beside them and write the person word in the empty box.
instruction.G3-399: Read the four words above the root word. Write the one that fits the sentence in the gap.

notes: Enlarged and read: the B peach (k-letters; reads as an apple), the B hen (a hen, fine), both sort cards (bins repeat the item picture; plum looks like an apple, apricot like an orange), both sequence stories (snowman, cake; orders unique), the B big/small dogs (same puppy at nearly the same size), the sound-box pictures fish/duck/dog/pig (dog is a puppy), the g1 question-word pictures (chef, florist), the 'next' story B (paper chain), the B pronoun pictures, the flute, the lizard + cursive card, the photographer card, and the student copies of k-letters part 3 (no empty line exists) and k-first-words part 3 (only 'whales' dashed).

US English: 'brackets' (g2 verb forms) should be 'parentheses' — the verb is shown in ( ); 'grey' should be 'gray'; 'garden' for where a child runs reads British, 'yard' is the US word; 'little green can' should be 'watering can'. No other British forms found in the ten dumps.
Picture-naming risk in sound and a/an tasks repeats the earlier review's finding: the cleanest fix for all of them is that the teacher names each picture (directions given for K-288, G1-312, G1-305).
g1-words-and-how-they-work prints on four pages per form with part 8 alone on page 4; packing parts 6-8 onto page 3 would save paper. Nothing is cut off or overlapping in any of the ten units.

The dump's worksheet names 'Sight Word in Sentences: {UNIT}', 'Spelling Rules: {UNIT}' and '{U} Fact File' carry unfilled placeholders; they do not print on the check pages, but make sure they never reach a printed label.
a/an appears in the K unit (L.1.1.h is a Grade 1 standard); it is the unit's own lesson, so I judged the check against the unit, not the standard.
